<reason>Side A (CON) won by converting Side B's overtime-threshold reframe into a concession: if the fifth day survives at a premium, the mandate's guaranteed effect in hour-intensive sectors is a higher wage bill, and its promised effect (an actual four-day week) arrives only where slack already exists. A answered B's pressure questions directly with the German sectoral-bargaining example and the "productivity first, then hours" sequence, and the distinction that historical hours laws lacked a statutory pay-freeze clause. B's answers were honest (deliberately chosen higher public spending, premium-plus-default-shift for the carer) and its "status quo isn't free / who pays in what currency" reframe was genuinely strong, keeping a live route alive. But A's "visibility is not capacity" and "redundant where it works, harmful where it bites" crystallization gave the cleaner reason to vote, and A's pressure question on funding exposed a burden B only partially discharged. Both sides used proper Q/A structure and avoided fake precision, though several turns were clipped at word limits.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A2.1: Side A seized on B2.3's "employers simply pay overtime or hire" concession, showing PRO cannot simultaneously claim output holds and nothing gets more expensive — either the shift disappears (patient absorbs it) or it stays (taxpayer absorbs it). B's recovery in B4.3 (premium as a real raise plus default-flip over a generation) was the debate's most honest exchange but remained partially concessive against A's closing that this is "the entire delivered content" for the sectors the motion aimed to rescue.</best_rebuttal>
